short: The slump that broke the post-war settlement and carried extremists into power.
full:
The Wall Street collapse that began on 24 October 1929 wiped out a decade of speculative gains within weeks, but the crash was as much symptom as cause. Bank failures destroyed deposits, the money supply contracted sharply, and the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 helped shrink world trade by roughly two-thirds. American loans that had been propping up German reparations payments were called in. By 1932 unemployment stood near a quarter of the workforce in the United States and at around six million in Germany.

The political consequences mattered more than the economic ones. The Nazi share of the vote rose from 2.6 per cent in 1928 to 37.3 per cent in July 1932, and Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933. Japan, hit hard by the collapse of the silk trade, turned towards expansion in Manchuria. Governments abandoned the gold standard, rearmament became a form of public works, and the assumptions on which the 1919 settlement rested did not survive the decade.
